keyPoints: A hot work permit is required before any welding, cutting, grinding, brazing, or open-flame operation in a construction area. The permit must be obtained from the authority having jurisdiction (GC, fire marshal, or site safety).
All combustible materials must be cleared or protected within 35 feet of the hot work area before work begins — move materials, cover with fire-resistant blankets, or wet them down.
A fire extinguisher must be immediately available at the hot work location throughout the operation.
A fire watch must be maintained during hot work and for a minimum of 30 minutes after work stops — longer if the work area has materials that can smolder.
Hot work must not be performed in areas where flammable vapors, gases, or dust may be present without atmospheric testing confirming the area is safe.
Cutting or grinding near electrical equipment, insulation, or conduit filled with combustible material requires extra protection and often a separate permit.
All openings, cracks, and penetrations in the work area through which sparks or slag could pass must be sealed or protected before hot work begins.

policies.source: PreTaskIQ Baseline | OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P
policies.title: Excavation & Trenching — Baseline Policy
policies.summary: Excavations require a competent person inspection before entry, a protective system at 5 feet of depth, and egress within 25 feet of all workers at 4 feet of depth. Visual judgment by untrained crew is not a substitute for competent person soil classification.
keyPoints: A competent person must classify soil type and inspect the excavation before each shift's work begins, and after any condition that could increase hazards — rain, vibration, nearby equipment operation, visible cracking.
Excavations 5 feet or deeper require a protective system (sloping, benching, shoring, or trench box/shield) before entry — no exceptions unless made entirely in stable rock.
Protective equipment present on site must actually be deployed once the depth threshold is reached — its presence on site does not satisfy the requirement.
Spoil piles, equipment, and materials must be kept at least 2 feet back from the edge of the excavation.
A safe means of egress (ladder, ramp, or steps) must be within 25 feet of all employees in excavations 4 feet or deeper.
Atmospheric testing is required before entry where a hazardous atmosphere exists or could reasonably exist.

For shallow, clearly no-entry excavations (under 3 feet, skid steer or equipment only), competent person, egress ladder, and trench protection questions do not apply — ask about utility strike and equipment clearance only.
Incremental depth increases over multiple days require the same inspection rigor as a trench excavated to full depth on day one.

policies.title: Aerial and Elevated Work Platforms — Baseline Policy
policies.summary: Aerial and elevated work platforms require pre-use inspections, appropriate fall protection, and prohibited use restrictions. Ground conditions must be evaluated before positioning any aerial lift.
keyPoints: A pre-use inspection must be performed before operating any aerial work platform each shift — including boom lifts, scissor lifts, and personnel lifts.
Boom lifts require a personal fall arrest system (harness and lanyard) anchored to the manufacturer-designated anchor point inside the platform. Guardrails alone are not sufficient in boom lifts.
Scissor lifts may use guardrails as fall protection per manufacturer guidance, but workers must stay within the platform boundaries — never lean over or reach past the guardrails.
Standing on the platform guardrails, using a ladder inside the platform to gain height, or otherwise exceeding the platform's working height is prohibited.
Ground conditions must be evaluated before positioning the lift — outriggers must be on solid, level ground with appropriate pads; operation on slopes exceeding manufacturer limits is prohibited.
Aerial lifts must not be moved with workers in the elevated position unless the manufacturer specifically authorizes it for that model.
Platform capacity — including workers, tools, and materials — must not exceed the manufacturer's rated load.
Operators must be trained and authorized on the specific type and model of aerial lift they are operating.

policies.source: PreTaskIQ Baseline | OSHA Heat Illness Prevention Guidance / Cal/OSHA T8 CCR 3395
policies.title: Heat Illness Prevention — Baseline Policy
policies.summary: Work in high-heat conditions requires scheduled rest, shade, and water breaks based on heat index thresholds, not individual discretion. Workers must feel empowered and expected to stop at first signs of heat-related symptoms.
keyPoints: Cool drinking water must be available at or near the work location — at least 1 quart per worker per hour during high-heat conditions. Workers should drink before they feel thirsty.

Rest and shade breaks must be scheduled based on heat index thresholds, not left to individual discretion: at heat index above 91°F, rest breaks every hour; above 103°F, mandatory cool-down rest periods apply.
Shade structures must be provided at outdoor work locations where shade is not otherwise available during high-heat periods.
New or returning workers require an acclimatization period — beginning with no more than 20% of normal work intensity on day one in high-heat conditions, increasing gradually over 7-14 days.
All crew members must be trained to recognize early heat illness symptoms — heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea, cramping — in themselves and coworkers.
Stopping work at the first signs of heat stress is the expected and supported response. No worker should feel pressured to continue through symptoms to maintain productivity.
Heat stroke is a medical emergency — call 911 immediately. Symptoms include confusion, lack of sweating despite heat, hot and dry skin, rapid heartbeat, loss of consciousness.
Water, rest, and shade are the three primary controls. All three must be in place during high-heat conditions, not just one or two of them.

policies.source: PreTaskIQ Baseline | OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC / ASME B30
policies.title: Crane, Hoist & Rigging — Baseline Policy
policies.summary: Crane and hoist operations require a certified or qualified operator, a pre-shift inspection, a qualified rigger for rigging operations, and an established exclusion zone. Power line clearance is mandatory before any lift near overhead lines.
keyPoints: Crane operators must be certified or qualified under a recognized accreditation process appropriate to the type and capacity of the equipment they operate.
A pre-shift inspection is required before each shift of crane use, with a more thorough periodic inspection at manufacturer-specified intervals.
A qualified rigger must supervise or perform rigging for any operation where employees are exposed to the hazards of the rigging.
An exclusion zone must be established around the swing radius and load path before any lift begins — unauthorized personnel must be barricaded out of the zone, not just warned.
Power line proximity: minimum clearance of 10 feet for lines up to 50kV, and greater clearance for higher voltages. Contact the utility before working within 20 feet of any overhead line.

A pre-lift plan is required for critical lifts — defined as lifts over 75% of rated capacity, tandem lifts, lifts over occupied areas, or lifts where the load is not visible to the operator throughout.
A signal person is required whenever the operator cannot see the load, the path of the load, or the landing zone.
Never exceed the rated load chart for the crane's current configuration, boom angle, and radius.

policies.source: PreTaskIQ Baseline | OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart E / 1910.132
policies.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) — Baseline Policy
policies.summary: Minimum baseline PPE is required in all active work areas, with task-specific PPE added based on the hazard analysis. PPE must be selected to match the specific hazard, not just a general category.
keyPoints: Baseline PPE for all active work areas: hard hat, ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses, high-visibility vest or shirt, and ASTM F2413 steel- or composite-toe boots. Hard hat class is only specified when required by a specific exposure or company policy — do not state a class unless the task involves electrical work near energized conductors, arc flash proximity, or a policy that mandates a specific class.

Gloves must be selected for the specific task hazard — cut-resistant for sharp edges, dielectric for electrical work, impact-resistant for hand-tool work, chemical-resistant for chemical exposure. General work gloves are not a substitute when a specific hazard is present.

Arc-rated / FR clothing is required for any work on or near energized electrical equipment where arc flash risk has not been eliminated. The FR rating must match the incident energy level from the arc-flash risk assessment.
Hard hats (not bump caps) are required when working at elevation with any overhead material handling or fall risk. A bump cap does not provide impact protection from above.
PPE must be inspected before each use. Damaged or defective PPE must be removed from service — it should not be used even for a short task.
Task-specific PPE identified in the hazard analysis always supersedes the baseline — baseline is a floor, not a ceiling.

Removing gloves for a task requiring dexterity must be evaluated against the specific hazard; 'better grip without gloves' is not by itself sufficient justification when pinch points, sharp edges, or heavy components are involved.
Hearing protection is required in areas where noise levels exceed 85 dBA — power tools, generators, and compressors frequently exceed this threshold.

policies.title: Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) Procedure
policies.summary: All work on equipment with potential for unexpected energization, start-up, or release of stored energy requires lockout/tagout before work begins.
keyPoints: Every employee exposed to the hazard must apply their own personal lock and tag — locking out at the panel/disconnect level alone is not sufficient; individual lock verification is mandatory before work begins under any group or panel lockout.
A zero-energy verification (try-before-you-rely) must be performed after lockout and before starting work: attempt to operate the equipment to confirm it will not start.
Only the employee who applied a lock may remove it. Locks may never be removed by another person except through the documented lock-removal-in-absence procedure with supervisor and safety sign-off.
Multi-employee lockout requires a group lockout device (lock box) so each worker's individual lock is on the box, not just the equipment.

Equipment must remain locked out for the entire duration of work, including breaks. Equipment is never to be temporarily re-energized to 'test' something without going through a full re-energization and re-lockout cycle.

Before re-energizing, the area must be inspected to confirm tools are removed, guards reinstalled, and all employees are clear, and all employees who applied locks must be accounted for and notified before locks are removed.
relatedPermits: Energized Work Permit (if LOTO cannot be achieved)

policies.title: Fall Protection Policy
policies.summary: Fall protection is required for any work performed at 6 feet or more above a lower level, and is recommended as best practice below that threshold when other risk factors are present.
keyPoints: Any work at or above 6 feet requires fall protection: guardrails, personal fall arrest systems (PFAS), or fall restraint, selected based on the specific task and anchor point availability.

Ladders: extension and straight ladders must extend at least 3 feet above the landing surface and be secured against displacement. Three points of contact must be maintained at all times. Heavy materials should not be hand-carried up a ladder; use a hoist, rope, or material lift where available.
Platform/step ladders are limited to the duty rating listed by the manufacturer; standing on the top two rungs/steps of a step ladder is prohibited.

Scissor lifts and aerial lifts require fall protection per manufacturer specification and site-specific JHA; guardrails alone may be sufficient in a scissor lift per manufacturer guidance, but operators must never climb on guardrails or use ladders inside the platform to gain extra height.
Hard hats (not bump caps) are required whenever work involves elevation combined with overhead material handling or any risk of head impact from a fall.
Floor and wall openings, including temporary openings created during the work shift, must be covered, guarded, or barricaded immediately — leaving an opening unprotected even briefly is a violation.
relatedPermits: Working at Heights Permit (site-specific, if required)

policies.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) Policy
policies.summary: Minimum baseline PPE is required on all active work sites, with task-specific PPE added based on the hazard analysis for the work being performed.
keyPoints: Baseline PPE for all site personnel in active work areas: hard hat, safety glasses, high-visibility vest/shirt/coat, and steel-toe boots. Hard hat class is specified only when required by a specific task exposure or company policy.
Gloves are required for material handling, sharp-edge work, and any task involving pinch points; glove type (cut-resistant, dielectric, chemical-resistant) must match the specific hazard.

Arc-rated/FR clothing and appropriate arc-flash PPE category gear is required for any work on or near energized electrical equipment where arc flash risk has not been eliminated through de-energization.

Hand protection should not be removed for dexterity tasks without a documented task-specific risk assessment; 'better grip without gloves' is not, by itself, sufficient justification to forgo hand protection on tasks involving pinch points, sharp edges, or heavy components.
PPE must be inspected before each use and removed from service if damaged.
Site-specific or task-specific PPE requirements identified in a hazard analysis always supersede baseline PPE — baseline is a floor, not a ceiling.

policies.title: Energized Electrical Work Policy
policies.summary: Work on electrical equipment must default to a de-energized state; energized work is permitted only when de-energization is infeasible and is governed by a separate energized work permit.
keyPoints: De-energization and LOTO is the default requirement for all electrical work. Energized work is the exception, not a default convenience.

Energized work requires a documented Energized Electrical Work Permit, justification for why de-energization is infeasible, arc-flash risk assessment, and approval from the responsible electrical safety supervisor before work begins.

Phase verification (confirming correct phase rotation/connection) must be independently performed by a second qualified person before any switch-over from temporary or test power to primary power, or vice versa — single-person phase verification is not permitted for primary power switching operations.
Testing for absence of voltage must be performed with a properly rated meter immediately before contact, and the meter must be verified on a known live source before and after the test.

Crews must not allow schedule pressure from clients, GCs, or other trades to shortcut energy-isolation, verification, or permit steps. Any team member may stop work to complete these steps regardless of external timeline pressure.

policies.title: Material Handling & Rigging Policy
policies.summary: Manual and mechanical material handling tasks must account for load weight, pinch points, and communication between team members moving shared loads.
keyPoints: Loads over 50 lbs being moved manually at elevation should use a mechanical aid (hoist, lift, rope-and-pulley) rather than hand-carrying, where one is available.
Two-person or team lifts require a designated lead who calls movement ('ready, lifting, moving') so all team members know when a shared load will move and where their hands should be positioned.

Before disassembling or repositioning any structure, panel, or framed component, verify that all fasteners are present and secure — do not assume a component will hold its own weight based on prior experience with similar components without first checking this specific item.
Any equipment, panel, or component found with missing, loose, or incomplete fasteners or hardware must be tagged immediately and reported, even if it is not part of today's task.
Pinch point hazards must be explicitly discussed before any multi-person handling of rigid or framed structures, including routine or frequently repeated tasks.
relatedPermits: Rigging Plan (for mechanical lifts above a threshold weight, per site requirements)

policies.title: Stop Work Authority Policy
policies.summary: Every employee, regardless of role or tenure, has the authority and obligation to stop work when an unsafe condition or uncertainty about safe execution is identified.
keyPoints: Any employee may stop work without fear of retaliation if they identify a hazard, an incomplete safety step, or are uncertain whether work can proceed safely.

If work conditions change from what was planned in the day's hazard analysis (new hazard, different task scope, new personnel, equipment change), work must stop and the hazard analysis must be reviewed and updated before continuing.
Asking a clarifying question before proceeding, including questions about lockout status, permit status, or PPE requirements, is expected and positive behavior, not a sign of inadequate training.
Stop-work events should be reported to a supervisor and, where relevant, logged so the organization can learn from the underlying condition that triggered the stoppage.

policies.title: Excavation & Trenching Policy
policies.summary: Excavations and trenches require a documented competent-person inspection and an appropriate protective system based on depth and soil conditions before any employee enters.
keyPoints: Any excavation 5 feet or deeper requires a protective system (sloping, benching, shoring, or a trench box/shield) before entry, unless the excavation is made entirely in stable rock.

A competent person must classify soil type and inspect the excavation before each shift's work begins, and again after any condition that could increase hazards (rain, vibration, nearby equipment operation, visible cracking).
Protective systems present on site must be deployed once the depth threshold is reached — equipment being available does not satisfy the requirement; it must actually be in use.
Spoil piles and other materials must be kept at least 2 feet back from the edge of any excavation.
A safe means of egress (ladder, ramp, or steps) must be within 25 feet of all employees working in excavations 4 feet or deeper.
Atmospheric testing is required before entry into excavations where a hazardous atmosphere exists or could reasonably be expected.
relatedPermits: Confined Space Entry Permit (if atmospheric hazard applicable)

policies.title: Mobile Equipment & Yard Traffic Policy
policies.summary: Mobile equipment operations in active work areas require spotters for limited-visibility maneuvers and physical separation from pedestrian traffic where practical.
keyPoints: A spotter is required for any reversing or blind-spot maneuver in an area with active foot traffic, stacked material, or limited sightlines — a functioning backup alarm alone does not satisfy this requirement.
Designated pedestrian paths, physically separated from active equipment travel lanes, must be established and marked in yards or laydown areas with regular mixed traffic.
Only trained and authorized operators may operate mobile equipment (skid steers, forklifts, excavators, loaders); authorization must be verifiable on request.
Equipment must come to a complete stop and sound a horn before beginning any reversing movement in an active work area.
Material stacking and storage should avoid creating blind corners along known travel paths; if unavoidable, the area must be treated as a spotter-required zone.

policies.title: Heat Illness Prevention Policy
policies.summary: Work in high-heat conditions requires scheduled rest, shade, and water breaks, with workers expected and supported to stop at the first signs of heat-related symptoms.
keyPoints: A scheduled rest-shade-water rotation must be established and followed when heat index or temperature thresholds are met, not left to individual discretion.
Cool drinking water must be readily accessible at the work location, with workers encouraged to hydrate before thirst is felt, not only when it is.
Workers new to high-heat conditions, or returning after time away, require a gradual acclimatization period rather than full-intensity work on day one of elevated temperatures.
All crew members must be trained to recognize early signs of heat-related illness (heavy sweating, dizziness, nausea, confusion, cramping) in themselves and coworkers.
Stopping work at early heat-stress symptoms is the expected and supported response — no employee should feel pressured to continue working through symptoms to avoid slowing down the crew.
Shade structures or shaded rest areas must be provided for exposed work locations (roofs, slabs, open yards) during high-heat periods.

policies.title: Respiratory Protection & Dust Control Policy
policies.summary: Tasks generating airborne dust, including concrete cutting and grinding, require engineering dust controls and respirator selection matched to the specific exposure, regardless of task duration.
keyPoints: Concrete cutting, grinding, and similar dust-generating tasks require an engineering dust control method (water suppression or vacuum dust collection) appropriate to the tool and material — task duration does not exempt a task from this requirement.

Respirator selection must match the specific exposure scenario and cutting method; a basic dust mask is not an acceptable substitute for a properly selected respirator on tasks with known silica or other hazardous dust generation.
Enclosed or poorly ventilated spaces require additional ventilation or restricted use of dry-cutting methods, since airborne dust concentrates faster than in open-air work.
Employees performing tasks that may require respirator use must be included in a respiratory protection program, including fit testing where applicable.
Visible dust accumulation in a work area during or after a task is a sign that current controls are insufficient and should prompt an immediate review, not just cleanup.

policies.title: Vehicle & Site Traffic Policy
policies.summary: Vehicle movements in active construction areas, including deliveries, require spotters for backing maneuvers and clear communication of site layout to recurring vendors.
keyPoints: Backing maneuvers by any vehicle (delivery trucks, concrete trucks, personal vehicles) in active construction areas require a spotter, regardless of how familiar the driver believes they are with the site.

Site layout changes affecting vehicle staging, parking, or travel lanes must be communicated to recurring delivery vendors and subcontractors before the change takes effect, not discovered on arrival.
Spotter-required zones must be marked with visible signage at site entrances and staging areas.
Large vehicle deliveries should be scheduled outside of shift-change windows where feasible, given increased pedestrian activity during those periods.
Any vehicle-to-structure or vehicle-to-equipment contact, even without injury, must be reported and reviewed as a near-miss for potential struck-by exposure.

policies.title: Aerial Work Near Energized Lines — Baseline Policy
policies.summary: Workers performing aerial tasks near energized power lines must maintain minimum approach distances at all times. Unqualified workers may not enter the limited approach boundary. Utility coordination is required before work within the limited approach boundary.
keyPoints: Minimum approach distance for unqualified workers: 10 feet from lines up to 50kV. Fiber installation crews are typically unqualified workers under OSHA 1910.269 and must maintain this distance.
The bucket truck boom, platform, workers, tools, and materials must all stay outside the minimum approach distance for all positions during the work.
A dedicated spotter must monitor clearance distance whenever an aerial platform operates near energized lines.
Contact the utility before work begins. Confirm line status, obtain clearance if work requires closer approach, and get written authorization before entering the limited approach boundary.
If work cannot be completed while maintaining MAD the work must stop and the utility must be contacted to arrange de-energization or protective measures.

procedures.name: Lockout/Tagout (LOTO)

steps.title: Verify the signed Method of Procedure (MOP) and review it with the crew
steps.description: Confirm the Method of Procedure (MOP) for this work has been signed off, then walk through it with every crew member who will help carry it out before any isolation begins, so everyone knows the sequence, the isolation points, and who does what.

steps.title: Confirm the Energy Isolation Permit (EIP)
steps.description: Confirm the Energy Isolation Permit (EIP) for this equipment was submitted and signed off ahead of the task, and note the devices and lock numbers it lists. Work does not start without it.

steps.title: Notify affected personnel
steps.description: Notify all employees who will be affected that equipment is being shut down and locked out for the work.

steps.title: Identify all energy sources
steps.description: Identify every energy source for the equipment (electrical, stored mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, gravity) — not just the primary disconnect.

steps.title: Shut down equipment
steps.description: Shut down the equipment using its normal stopping procedure.

steps.title: Isolate energy sources
steps.description: Operate the energy-isolating device(s) (breaker, disconnect, valve) so the equipment is disconnected from all energy sources. Confirm each device matches the Energy Isolation Permit before locks are applied.

steps.title: Apply individual locks and tags
steps.description: Every employee exposed to the hazard applies their own personal lock and tag. Locking out at the panel/disconnect level alone is not sufficient — for group lockout, each worker's lock goes on the lock box, not just the equipment. Record each lock number on the Energy Isolation Permit.

steps.title: Relieve stored energy
steps.description: Relieve, restrain, or otherwise render safe any stored or residual energy (capacitors, springs, elevated parts, pressurized systems).

steps.title: Verify zero energy
steps.description: Verify zero energy before work starts. For electrical equipment, use a Live-Dead-Live test: check the voltage tester on a known live source, test the equipment for zero voltage, then re-check the tester on the same known source. For other energy types, attempt to operate the equipment using normal controls to confirm it will not start. This step cannot be skipped even if isolation seemed successful.

steps.title: Perform the work
steps.description: Work may now proceed. Equipment must remain locked out for the entire duration of work, including breaks. Do not temporarily re-energize to 'test' something without a full re-energization and re-lockout cycle.

steps.title: Inspect before re-energizing and release the Energy Isolation Permit
steps.description: Before removing locks, confirm the work scope is complete: tools removed, guards and covers reinstalled, and all employees clear. Then release the Energy Isolation Permit.

steps.title: Account for all lock holders and remove locks
steps.description: Notify all employees who applied locks before removal. Only the employee who applied a lock may remove it, except through the documented lock-removal-in-absence procedure with supervisor and safety sign-off.

steps.title: Re-energize
steps.description: Restore energy to the equipment and notify affected personnel that the equipment is back in service.

procedures.criticalStepNote: Steps 7 (individual lock application), 9 (zero-energy verification), and 12 (accounting for all lock holders) are the steps most often skipped or rushed in real incidents — flag these especially hard if reported out of order or skipped. Hold points from the permit: stop work if unexpected energy is found, if the equipment has been modified since the permit was issued, or if circuits or equipment not listed on the permit are affected. Work is not authorized past a hold point until the issue is resolved.

procedures.name: Energized Electrical Work Permit

steps.title: Confirm de-energization is infeasible
steps.description: Document the specific justification for why this work cannot be performed de-energized. De-energization and LOTO remain the default; energized work is the exception.

steps.title: Complete arc-flash risk assessment
steps.description: Determine incident energy level and required arc-rated PPE category for the specific task and equipment.

steps.title: Obtain Energized Electrical Work Permit approval
steps.description: Get sign-off from the responsible electrical safety supervisor before work begins. The permit requires this approval before any energized work starts, not after.

steps.title: Don arc-rated PPE
steps.description: PPE must match the incident energy level determined in Step 2, not a generic baseline.

steps.title: Test for absence of voltage (if applicable to the task)
steps.description: Use a properly rated meter, verified on a known live source immediately before and after the test.

steps.title: Independent phase verification (for any primary power switch-over)
steps.description: A second qualified person must independently verify phase connection/rotation before any switch-over from temporary or test power to primary power, or vice versa. Single-person phase verification is not permitted for this step.

steps.title: Perform the energized work
steps.description: Proceed with the work under the approved permit conditions. Any team member may stop work if conditions change, regardless of schedule pressure from clients, GCs, or other trades.

steps.title: Close out the permit
steps.description: Confirm work is complete, equipment is in its intended final state, and close out the energized work permit.

procedures.criticalStepNote: Step 3 (permit approval before starting) and Step 6 (independent phase verification before any switch-over) map directly to real incidents — work proceeding without permit approval, or a single person verifying phase under time pressure. Flag these hardest if skipped or rushed.

steps.title: Obtain entry permit signed by entry supervisor before approaching the opening
Set up traffic control and barricades around the manhole opening
Test atmosphere for oxygen, combustible gases (LEL), H2S and CO before opening cover
Open cover — stand upwind, do not lean over the opening
Ventilate with forced-air blower minimum 5 minutes before entry
Re-test atmosphere after ventilation — confirm all readings acceptable
Designate attendant — stationed at opening, in communication, does not enter
Confirm rescue plan in place before entry — rescue services identified and reachable
Entrant descends using approved access — maintain 3-point contact on ladder
Continuous atmospheric monitoring throughout occupancy
Entrant exits — attendant confirms all personnel clear before closing cover
